D1.1.1a.q: Police seize a suspect's phone at the scene. What should they do to stop it being remotely wiped?
options: Put it in a Faraday bag
Switch it off and on again
Connect it to the station Wi-Fi
D1.1.1a.why: A Faraday bag blocks signals, so the device can't be remotely wiped or changed. Then the chain of custody is recorded.

D1.1.1b.q: An investigator must examine a hard drive without changing the original evidence. What should they do first?
options: Make a forensic image and analyse the copy
Open the files directly on the original
D1.1.1b.why: Investigators make an exact bit-for-bit image and work on the copy, keeping the original intact.

D1.1.2.q: An attacker's malware is running only in a server's memory. Why is it hard to collect evidence of it?
options: RAM contents are lost when the system powers off
Memory can't be copied at all
D1.1.2.why: Live forensics must capture volatile data such as RAM before it is lost, without altering the system.

D1.1.3.q: After a breach, an investigator reviews firewall and router logs to trace where the attacker connected from. What type of forensics is this?
D1.1.3.why: Network forensics collects and analyses evidence from network devices.

D1.1.4.q: Before touching anything, an investigator photographs the desk, sketches where devices sit and writes timed notes. What are they doing?
D1.1.4.why: The scene must be recorded thoroughly at the time, with photos, diagrams and contemporaneous notes.

D2.1.1.q: An investigator images a drive and records its hash value before and after analysis. Why?
options: To prove the evidence hasn't changed
D2.1.1.why: Matching hashes prove the snapshot is identical to the original, so it can be relied on.

D2.1.2.q: Every action in an investigation is logged with who did it and when. What is the main purpose?
options: So the evidence is reliable and can stand up in court
D2.1.2.why: Recording every finding and action keeps evidence reliable and defensible.

D2.1.3.q: An investigator accidentally opens a file on the original drive, changing its 'last accessed' date. What must happen?
options: The change must be recorded, as it may affect admissibility
Nothing, as small changes don't matter
D2.1.3.why: Altered data may be inadmissible, so every change must be recorded. Ideally, investigators work only on a copy.

D2.2.1.q: An investigation finds a member of staff emailed customer records to a personal account. What must the investigator decide?
options: Whether this is a crime, a legal (GDPR) breach or a policy breach
How to speed up the network
D2.2.1.why: Findings are assessed to decide whether they show a crime, a legal breach, a policy breach or another incident.

D2.2.2.q: Overnight, a server sends large amounts of data to an unknown foreign IP, and failed logins spike. What do these suggest?
D2.2.2.why: Unusual outbound traffic, failed login spikes and odd DNS requests are signs of compromise.

D2.3.q: After an incident, the investigator writes a document explaining what happened and recommending new training and policies. What is this?
D2.3.why: A security report analyses the incident and recommends how to stop it happening again.
